children.title: "Premature Anti-Fascists": the Lincoln Brigade & Its Punishments (1937–1955)
children.body:
The 2,800 American volunteers who fought Franco in the Abraham Lincoln Brigade broke the Neutrality Act to do it, and the state never forgave them. Volunteers were prosecuted and imprisoned over the passports they traveled on; recruiters faced federal charges; and returning veterans found themselves branded — in the phrase they wore as a badge — "premature anti-fascists": surveilled by the FBI, purged from wartime officer candidacy, hauled before HUAC and the Subversive Activities Control Board for decades.

Brigade veterans thread through this database's later cases — Smith Act defendants like Robert Thompson, whose Guadalcanal Distinguished Service Cross did not spare him prison; blacklisted seamen and union men; Bill Bailey and Harry Bridges' comrades of the waterfront. Their treatment established the American rule that fighting fascism too early was punished longer than collaborating with it ever was.

children.title: Fighting the Bund & the Silver Shirts (1933–1941)
children.body:
When German-American Bund rallies and Silver Shirt organizing spread through the 1930s, the police protected the fascists and arrested their opponents. At the Bund's 20,000-strong 1939 "Pro-American Rally" in Madison Square Garden — swastikas beside Washington — the plumber Isadore Greenbaum rushed the stage against George Lincoln Rockwell's forerunners, was beaten by stormtroopers and police alike, and fined for disorderly conduct: the night's only person charged. Outside, mounted police clubbed fifty thousand anti-fascist protesters.

In Minneapolis, Teamster Local 544's union defense guard — organized by the same Trotskyists later jailed in the first Smith Act case — broke the Silver Shirts' organizing drive in 1938 without a single arrest of a fascist; the union's armed self-defense became, instead, evidence in the government's 1941 prosecution of its leaders. The pattern — anti-fascists in the dock, fascists under escort — is the movement's founding grievance.

children.title: The Greensboro Massacre & the Prosecutions That Followed (1979–1985)
children.body:
On November 3, 1979, Klansmen and Nazis drove into a "Death to the Klan" march organized by the Communist Workers Party in Greensboro, North Carolina, and shot five organizers dead on camera — Sandi Smith, Dr. Jim Waller, Bill Sampson, Cesar Cauce, and Dr. Michael Nathan. A police informant had ridden with the caravan and the police detail was absent; all-white juries acquitted the killers in both state and federal trials.

The only people jailed in the aftermath were survivors and their allies: march leader Nelson Johnson was arrested bleeding at the scene and charged with inciting riot, and CWP members faced prosecution while the shooters walked. A 1985 civil jury finally found Klansmen, Nazis, and Greensboro police jointly liable for one death — the sole official accountability ever imposed — and the case became the American movement's textbook on state collusion, later the subject of the country's first Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

children.title: The Anti-Klan Committees & Their Prisoners (1978–1990)
children.body:
Greensboro's lesson — that the state would not stop the Klan — drove the anti-Klan organizing of the 1980s. The John Brown Anti-Klan Committee, born from prisoner correspondence exposing Klan organizing among New York prison guards, confronted Klan rallies from Meriden to Austin; its militants absorbed arrests by the score, and its cadre overlapped the May 19th Communist Organization, whose imprisoned members — Linda Evans, Laura Whitehorn, Marilyn Buck — counted anti-Klan work central to the politics they were jailed for.

In the same years, Klan and Nazi paramilitaries assembled openly at Camp Puller and Hayden Lake while prosecutors reached instead for the movement's opponents; when the federal government finally tried the white-supremacist leadership for sedition at Fort Smith in 1988, an all-white jury acquitted everyone — the mirror image, activists noted, of the sedition convictions handed to Puerto Rican and Black revolutionaries in the same decade.

children.title: The Modern Era: Charlottesville to the Antifa Prosecutions (2017– )
children.body:
The fascist revival of the Trump era renewed the old asymmetry. After Charlottesville, DeAndre Harris — beaten by white supremacists in a parking garage on video — was himself charged at a Klansman's instigation before acquittal; in New York, David Campbell served a year for fighting outside an alt-right gala in a prosecution his supporters contrasted with the wrist-slaps given the Proud Boys' assailants of the same season. Anarchist prisoner Eric King's decade in federal custody was extended by prosecutions his defense showed to be built on retaliation for his politics.

From the J20 mass indictment of 2017 — over 200 inauguration protesters charged with identical felonies before the cases collapsed — to the Atlanta RICO indictment's sweep of anti-fascist organizers, the era's record repeats the century's pattern: the movement against fascism, not fascism itself, remains the more reliably prosecuted.

children.title: The Los Angeles Eight (1987–2007)
children.body:
In January 1987 the INS arrested seven Palestinian students and the Kenyan wife of one — the Los Angeles Eight — and moved to deport them for distributing magazines and raising humanitarian funds associated with the PFLP: activity the FBI conceded would be legal for citizens, prosecuted under the McCarran-Walter Act's Cold War ideological-exclusion clauses. Khader Hamide and Michel Shehadeh spent the next twenty years fighting removal.

The case became the constitutional test of ideological deportation: courts repeatedly found the government had targeted the eight for protected speech, Congress repealed and replaced the statutes beneath the case, and in 2007 an immigration judge ended it as "an embarrassment to the rule of law." The LA 8 template — immigration law as the political weapon against Palestine activism — would return, undiminished, two decades later.

children.title: The Sami Al-Arian Case (2003–2015)
children.body:
Sami Al-Arian, a tenured computer-science professor at the University of South Florida and a prominent Muslim civil-rights advocate, was indicted in 2003 on 53 counts of supporting Palestinian Islamic Jihad — the PATRIOT Act era's flagship material-support prosecution, built on half a million intercepted conversations from years of FISA surveillance. After a six-month 2005 trial, the jury acquitted him on the major counts and hung on the rest, convicting him of nothing.

The government refused the verdict's meaning: Al-Arian pleaded to a single count to end the case, expecting release, but was held in contempt for years more when he refused grand-jury testimony he believed was a perjury trap, spending five and a half years in prison and house arrest before his 2015 deportation to Turkey. His case remains the era's measure of how far a Palestine prosecution could run past a jury's refusal.

children.title: The Holy Land Five (2001–2009)
children.body:
The Holy Land Foundation was America's largest Muslim charity when the government shut it down in December 2001 and prosecuted its leaders for material support — not for funding violence, which was never alleged, but for charity to Palestinian zakat committees that the government itself, and USAID, had dealt with. The first trial ended in a hung jury; at the 2008 retrial, featuring an anonymous Israeli intelligence "expert" no defense could confront, all five were convicted.

Ghassan Elashi and Shukri Abu Baker received sixty-five years; Mufid Abdulqader, Abdulrahman Odeh, and Mohammad El-Mezain, terms of fifteen to twenty. The five — men who fed orphans through committees never designated as terrorist — became the Palestine movement's central prisoners, their case cited across the civil-liberties spectrum as the criminalization of Muslim charity itself.

children.title: Rasmea Odeh (2013–2017)
children.body:
Rasmea Odeh — associate director of Chicago's Arab American Action Network, organizer of hundreds of immigrant women — was prosecuted in 2013 for failing to disclose, on her decade-old naturalization forms, a 1969 Israeli military-court conviction obtained, she testified, through weeks of torture and sexual assault in Israeli custody. The unnaturalization case, brought after a federal investigation of Midwest Palestine activists produced nothing else, was understood by the movement as retribution for a life of organizing.

Convicted in 2014 in a trial where her torture evidence was excluded, she won a rare appellate reversal on that ground; facing retrial under new terrorism allegations, she accepted denaturalization and was deported to Jordan in 2017. Her farewell rally in Chicago, thousands strong, marked the case as the bridge between the LA 8 era and the campus repression to come.

children.title: The Encampments & the Deportation Campaign (2023– )
children.body:
The movement against the Gaza war brought the largest campus protest wave since Vietnam — and over 3,100 arrests in the spring of 2024 alone as encampments from Columbia to UCLA were cleared by riot police, followed by expulsions, felony prosecutions of Stop Cop City-style breadth in some states, and Congress's campaign against university administrations deemed insufficiently punitive.

In 2025 the government turned to the LA 8's old weapon at new scale: green-card holders and student-visa activists — Mahmoud Khalil taken from his Columbia apartment, Rümeysa Öztürk seized masked off a Somerville street over an op-ed, Mohsen Mahdawi at his citizenship interview, Badar Khan Suri at his home — detained for deportation on foreign-policy grounds for pro-Palestinian speech. Courts ordered each released through 2025, and in AAUP v. Rubio a federal judge held the ideological-deportation campaign unconstitutional — the LA 8 verdict, relearned under fire, in a struggle still unfolding.

children.title: The Molly Maguires (1876–1879)
children.body:
In the anthracite fields of Pennsylvania, the first great labor "terror" prosecution was a wholly private affair: the Reading Railroad's president hired the Pinkerton agency, whose operative James McParlan spent two years inside the Irish miners' lodges; the railroad's own attorneys then prosecuted the "Molly Maguires" before juries from which Irish Catholics were excluded, on McParlan's uncorroborated word. Twenty men were hanged between 1877 and 1879 — ten on a single day, June 21, 1877, "the Day of the Rope."

The condemned went to the gallows protesting their innocence; a century later Pennsylvania posthumously pardoned John Kehoe, acknowledging the trials as corporate vengeance against the miners' union movement. The Mollies stand first in this database's long line of labor's executed and imprisoned — the proof, at the tradition's origin, that in the coalfields the state's justice could be leased.

children.title: Debs, Pullman & Government by Injunction (1894–1895)
children.body:
When the American Railway Union's 1894 boycott of Pullman cars paralyzed the western railroads, the federal government broke it with the new weapon of the labor injunction — a court order against the strike itself — enforced by 12,000 troops who left some thirty workers dead. Eugene Debs and the ARU leadership were imprisoned for six months at Woodstock, Illinois, not for any crime but for contempt of the injunction; the Supreme Court's In re Debs blessed the procedure, and "government by injunction" ruled labor relations for forty years.

Debs entered Woodstock a trade unionist and left it a socialist, reading his way to the politics that would later earn him the Espionage Act's ten-year sentence. The Pullman prisoners established the pattern of the era: the strike leader jailed by judicial decree, without jury, whenever labor won too much.

children.title: The Criminal-Syndicalism Era (1917–1937)
children.body:
Between 1917 and 1920, more than twenty states passed criminal-syndicalism laws making membership in a union that advocated "industrial change by force" a felony — statutes aimed at the IWW and used against communists and strike organizers for two decades. California alone prosecuted over 500 people and imprisoned 128 at San Quentin and Folsom, from Charlotte Anita Whitney to the entire leadership of the 1930s agricultural strikes; the Imperial Valley and Sacramento conspiracy trials filled this database with farm-labor prisoners.

Idaho, Washington, Oregon, and Kansas ran parallel campaigns, and Oklahoma's statute jailed Communist organizers into the 1930s. Only in DeJonge v. Oregon (1937) and the slow repeal era did the laws recede — after establishing, for a generation of American workers, that the union card itself could be the indictment.

children.title: The CIO Era: Little Steel, Memorial Day & the Strike Prosecutions (1936–1941)
children.body:
The CIO's organizing explosion met the old machinery at full force. On Memorial Day 1937, Chicago police fired into a crowd of Republic Steel strikers and their families, killing ten — shot mostly in the back, as suppressed newsreel footage showed — and wounding a hundred; the only people prosecuted were sixty-five strikers, charged while the La Follette Committee documented the massacre from the police's own films. Across the Little Steel towns, National Guard occupations and mass arrests broke the 1937 strike; in Massillon and Youngstown, strikers were killed and their leaders jailed.

The same years jailed sit-down strikers by the hundreds and sent tenant-farmer and packinghouse organizers to southern chain gangs. The La Follette hearings' four million words on industrial espionage, private arsenals, and strike-breaking remain the fullest official record of what American labor's freedom cost.

children.title: Taft-Hartley & the Anticommunist Purge of Labor (1947–1957)
children.body:
The Taft-Hartley Act's non-communist affidavit turned the Cold War inward on the unions: left-led internationals were expelled from the CIO, and their officers prosecuted for allegedly false affidavits — furriers' leader Ben Gold convicted in 1954, Mine-Mill's Maurice Travis and Clinton Jencks pursued through the decade, with Jencks v. United States (1957) finally forcing the government to show defendants their accusers' FBI reports. Harry Bridges was tried four times across two decades in the government's marathon effort to deport the longshore leader.

Deportation swept the foreign-born left of the labor movement — the ILWU Local 37 cannery leaders Chris Mensalvas and Ernesto Mangaoang among the era's defining cases — while Smith Act prosecutions took union communists from Maurice Braverman to the Flint auto militants. The purge broke industrial unionism's radical wing, and its prisoners fill this database's 1950s pages.

children.title: PATCO & the Criminalized Strike, Again (1981– )
children.body:
When 11,345 air-traffic controllers struck in August 1981, President Reagan fired them all, banned them from federal service for life, and had the union's leaders taken to court in chains: PATCO officers were jailed for contempt of back-to-work injunctions — strikers led away in handcuffs and leg irons before television cameras — and the union was decertified and fined into oblivion. The spectacle licensed a generation of employers to treat the strike itself as an offense.

The pattern persists wherever labor law meets the criminal code: injunction contempt against miners in the Pittston strike, mass arrests of Justice for Janitors and Fight for $15 civil disobedients, felony prosecutions of picket-line militants, and the routine arrest of union organizers from the fields of California to the warehouse gates — the century-old machinery of Debs's Woodstock, still in service.

children.title: George Jackson, the Soledad Brothers & the San Quentin Six (1970–1976)
children.body:
George Jackson — sentenced at eighteen to one-year-to-life for a $70 robbery, and kept eleven years by the indeterminate-sentence board as he became a revolutionary writer — was charged with two Soledad Brothers, Fleeta Drumgo and John Clutchette, in the 1970 death of a guard, days after a tower guard killed three Black prisoners with impunity. Soledad Brother made him the prison movement's voice worldwide; his seventeen-year-old brother Jonathan died raiding the Marin courthouse that August, the case that swept up Angela Davis, acquitted in 1972.

George Jackson was shot dead by San Quentin guards on August 21, 1971 — the surviving Soledad Brothers were acquitted months later — and six prisoners were then tried for the day's guard deaths in the 16-month San Quentin Six trial, shackled to the courtroom floor. The Jackson cases made "political prisoner" a category American courts could no longer pretend not to understand.

children.title: Attica & the Attica Brothers (1971–1976)
children.body:
The Attica uprising of September 9–13, 1971 — 1,281 prisoners holding the yard under an elected multiracial leadership, demanding minimum wage, religious freedom, and amnesty, three weeks after George Jackson's killing — ended when Governor Rockefeller ordered the assault in which state gunfire killed twenty-nine prisoners and ten hostages. Troopers' torture of survivors ran for days; the state then indicted only prisoners: sixty-two Attica Brothers on 1,289 counts, with defendants like Dacajeweiah (John Hill) convicted while every trooper walked.

The Attica Brothers' defense — a movement in itself — cracked the prosecution open when a state investigator, Malcolm Bell, exposed the cover-up of official crimes; Governor Carey closed the books with a 1976 amnesty, and decades of civil litigation ended with $12 million to the tortured survivors in 2000. Attica remains the word for both the prison movement's possibility and the state's answer.

children.title: The Angola 3 (1971–2016)
children.body:
At Louisiana's Angola — the plantation-turned-penitentiary — Albert Woodfox, Herman Wallace, and Robert King organized a Black Panther Party chapter inside the walls in 1971, against the prison's systematized rape economy and dollar-a-day field labor. When guard Brent Miller was killed in 1972, the organizers were convicted on testimony bought with cartons of cigarettes and promises of pardon; King was convicted of a separate killing on similar evidence. The three were then buried in solitary confinement — six-by-nine cells, twenty-three hours a day, for decades.

Robert King's conviction was overturned in 2001 after 29 years in solitary; Herman Wallace, dying of cancer, was freed by a federal judge in 2013 and died three days later; Albert Woodfox, his conviction thrice overturned, was released on his 69th birthday in 2016 after nearly 44 years in solitary — the longest such confinement in American history, and the case that put solitary itself on trial worldwide.

children.title: Marion, Lexington & the Control-Unit Fight (1972–2006)
children.body:
The state's answer to the prison movement was architectural: the control unit. Marion's H-Unit, built after the movement years, became in 1983 — following the killing of two guards — a permanent lockdown, the first prison in America run entirely on solitary confinement; its "Marion model" was exported to the states' supermaxes and perfected at ADX Florence, where the political prisoners of this database from Oscar López to the Green Scare's CMU inmates were concentrated. The Committee to End the Marion Lockdown, prisoners' writings, and UN condemnations built the case that the control unit is torture.

Its most notorious experiment was the Lexington High Security Unit, an underground isolation prison for women political prisoners — Susan Rosenberg, Silvia Baraldini, Alejandrina Torres — whose sensory-deprivation regime was closed by federal court order in 1988 after Amnesty International's intervention: the movement's one clean victory over the architecture of disappearance.

children.title: The Prison-Strike Era & Its Reprisals (2010– )
children.body:
The movement returned inside in the 2010s: Georgia's 2010 work stoppage, the Pelican Bay hunger strikes of 2011–13 — 30,000 refusing food at their peak, ending California's indefinite SHU terms — and the national prison strikes of 2016 and 2018, called by the Free Alabama Movement and Jailhouse Lawyers Speak against "prison slavery," the largest in American history. The organizers paid the traditional price: Alabama's Kinetik Justice (Robert Earl Council) spent years in solitary for organizing; Bennu Hannibal Ra-Sun (Melvin Ray) was buried in segregation without disciplinary charges; strike spokespeople nationwide were transferred, gassed, and isolated.

Their cases — with Ohio's death-row Lucasville organizers like Imam Siddique Abdullah Hasan, and writers punished for journalism from prison — form the newest generation in this database: prisoners made political prisoners by organizing against the prison itself, the movement's oldest and most exact definition.

children.title: Before Stonewall: a Criminalized People (1920s–1969)
children.body:
Until the 1960s ended, queer life in America was policed as crime itself: sodomy laws in every state — with sentences to life, and in California indefinite "sexual psychopath" commitment with lobotomies and forced ECT — masquerade laws jailing anyone in fewer than three articles of "gender-appropriate" clothing, and bar raids netting tens of thousands yearly, names printed in the papers. Henry Gerber, who founded the country's first gay-rights organization in Chicago in 1924, was arrested and broken within months; ONE magazine had to win at the Supreme Court in 1958 merely to be mailable.

Resistance predated the famous riot: Cooper Do-nuts in 1959, the Compton's Cafeteria rising of San Francisco's transgender street queens in 1966, the Black Cat protests of 1967 — each a revolt of the repeatedly arrested. The pre-Stonewall generations, jailed simply for existing, are the movement's uncounted political prisoners.

children.title: Stonewall, STAR & the Liberation Generation (1969–1974)
children.body:
The June 1969 Stonewall rebellion — six nights of the raided fighting back, street queens and homeless youth in front — turned the routine of arrest into the birth of a liberation movement. Its veterans Sylvia Rivera and Marsha P. Johnson, arrested more times than either could count ("I got my civil rights in a paddy wagon," Rivera said), founded STAR — Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries — housing the kids the movement and the city both abandoned, and carried the Young Lords' and Panthers' politics into gay liberation.

The Gay Liberation Front named itself for the NLF and marched for Panther prisoners; Huey Newton's 1970 letter welcomed the alliance. The generation's arrests — GAA zaps, the Rockefeller Five, Rivera dragged from the 1973 rally stage — established the movement's claim staked in this database: that the criminalization of queer and trans existence was political imprisonment by another name.

children.title: Queer Radicals of the Underground (1970s–2010s)
children.body:
The armed movements of the 1970s and 1980s carried an openly queer contingent whose members fill this database. The George Jackson Brigade's Rita Brown and Ed Mead were out in prison — Mead co-founding Men Against Sexism at Walla Walla to break the prison's rape trade; Black Liberation Army theorist Kuwasi Balagoon, bisexual and unapologetic, died of AIDS at Auburn in 1986; and the May 19th and resistance-conspiracy prisoners Laura Whitehorn, Linda Evans, and Susan Rosenberg organized as out lesbians through decades inside, fighting for HIV-positive prisoners at every institution that held them.

Their double stigma — revolutionaries in the prison, queers in the movement and the cellblock — made them bridges: the AIDS-in-prison organizing of the 1990s, the queer wing of today's prisoner-support networks, and the tradition by which anarchist queer and trans prisoners like Marius Mason are defended now, all descend from them.

children.title: ACT UP & the AIDS Civil Disobedience (1987–1996)
children.body:
Facing a plague the government met with silence, ACT UP made arrest its instrument: Wall Street 1987; the FDA seizure of 1988 that forced the drug-approval system open; "Stop the Church" at St. Patrick's in 1989, 111 arrests; the CDC, NIH, and the 1992 ashes action at the White House fence. Across a decade, AIDS activists absorbed thousands of arrests — ACT UP chapters treated jail support and "arrest-ready" affinity groups as core infrastructure — in the most sustained health-justice civil disobedience in American history.

The campaign's targets included the prisons themselves, where people with HIV were segregated and left to die untreated: ACT UP's prison committees, with the inside organizing of prisoners like the ACE women of Bedford Hills and the political prisoners of the resistance-conspiracy generation, forced the first HIV care behind bars. The movement lost a generation and changed medicine; its arrestees changed what protest could demand.

children.title: The Trans Prisoners' Struggle: CeCe McDonald to Chelsea Manning (2011– )
children.body:
The movement's current front is the trans prisoner. CeCe McDonald, a Black trans woman jailed in a men's prison in 2012 for surviving a neo-Nazi's attack with a fatal wound to her attacker, became the emblem of criminalized self-defense — "prisons aren't safe for anyone, and that's the key issue," she said on release. Ashley Diamond's suits against Georgia twice forced the federal courts to confront the rape and medical denial trans women face in men's prisons; Marius Mason's fight for treatment in federal custody set precedents from inside a terrorism sentence.

Chelsea Manning fused the threads: the whistleblower of the Iraq War logs came out upon sentencing in 2013, fought for and won transition care in a military prison, saw her 35-year sentence commuted in 2017 — and returned to jail in 2019–20 for a year of civil contempt, refusing a grand jury against WikiLeaks. The trans political prisoner, doubly caged, now stands where this movement's history began: punished for existing, organizing anyway.
